title: Self-Predictive Representations for Combinatorial Generalization in Behavioral Cloning
claim: Predicting future and past latent states with self-predictive objectives makes representations temporally consistent, so trajectories that intersect can be composed into novel start-goal pairs.
layout: 2 panels, left geometric sketch, right left-to-right diagram with stop-gradient marks
description: Two panels. Panel (a) is a toy sketch of two black trajectories that cross at a dot labeled w. One runs s0 to sh and the other runs sb to sf. Dashed green arrows labeled ψ link φ(s0) to φ(sw) and φ(sw) to φ(sf). A legend names φ as the representation and ψ as the predictor. This shows that training on two intersecting paths should let the model generalize to s0 → sf. Panel (b) is a block diagram of BYOL-γ. Green φ(s_t) and φ(s_{t+k}) blocks sit above a row of Ant-maze image frames. A purple ψ_f block takes φ(s_t) and action a_t. A purple ψ_b block takes φ(s_{t+k}). Two pink L loss boxes receive the predictions. Blue lines and double-slash marks denote stop-gradients. The eye goes first to the colored boxes on the right.
caption: \textbf{(\subref{fig:predictive}) Self-predictive Representations.} We consider training on trajectories like, $s_0 \rightarrow s_h$ and $s_b \rightarrow s_f$, which intersect at $w$, and then evaluating on a task like $s_0 \rightarrow s_f$, requiring combinatorial generalization. \textbf{(\subref{fig:byolg-diagram}) Representation learning with \methodbf.} We predict future state representations $\phi(s_{t+k})$ via $\psi_f(\phi(s_t), a)$, and also predict backwards with $\psi_b(\phi(s_{t+k}))$. The target offset is sampled geometrically: $k \sim geom(1 - \gamma)$. Stop-gradients are denoted by //. We provide more details on the training procedure $\mathcal{L}$ in Section [ref].
abstract: While goal-conditioned behavior cloning (GCBC) methods can perform well on in-distribution training tasks, they do not necessarily generalize zero-shot to tasks that require conditioning on novel state-goal pairs, i.e. combinatorial generalization. In part, this limitation can be attributed to a lack of temporal consistency in the state representation learned by BC; if temporally correlated states are properly encoded to similar latent representations, then the out-of-distribution gap for novel state-goal pairs would be reduced. We formalize this notion by demonstrating how encouraging long-range temporal consistency via successor representations (SR) can facilitate generalization. We then propose a simple yet effective representation learning objective, $\text{BYOL-}Î³$ for GCBC, which theoretically approximates the successor representation in the finite MDP case through self-predictive representations, and achieves competitive empirical performance across a suite of challenging tasks requiring combinatorial generalization.
